stories.title: Kenya: Young People Must Shape Their Own SRHR Future, Says Kenyan Activist
stories.summary: Kenya: Young People Must Shape Their Own SRHR Future, Says Kenyan Activist Karin Schermbrucker/UNICEF Adolescent girls and young women (AGYW) in Eastern and Southern Africa continue to face a disproportionate burden of HIV, early and unintended pregnancy, and poor sexual and reproductive health outcomesâparticularly during key life transitions such as leaving school, early pregnancy, migration, or exposure to violence. 6 October 2026 allAfrica.com By Melody Chironda Across Africa, young people are being told that their sexual and reproductive health and rights matter. But for many, accessing those rights remains a daily struggle. Progress on sexual and reproductive health and rights (SRHR) has been made by governments and health systems, but this progress is not equal. Many adolescents, particularly girls and young women, still face obstacles to accessing the information, services, and legal protection they need to make informed choices regarding their bodies and futures. Fear of being stigmatized and concerns about confidentiality and who to go to for help can also be reasons why young people are not able to access sexual and reproductive health information and services when they need them.

Photograph: Pamela Tulizo Congolese photographer Pamela Tulizo uses costume and vivid scenery to celebrate women’s strength and give a new perspective on slavery By Sarah Johnson P amela Tulizo’s latest series of photographs started with a question. “I asked myself, why are women in my community in particular, and African women in general, so strong?” says Tulizo, an artist and photographer from the Democratic Republic of the Congo . “Where does this strength come from?” Growing up in Goma in eastern DRC, Tulizo was informed and inspired by the women she was surrounded by, including her mother, her sisters, her mother’s friends and her neighbours. Years later, when she began to look into the role of women throughout African history, she says: “I realised that perhaps women have been forced to be strong since the dawn of time, forced by circumstance to build that resilience.” View image in fullscreen Women are placed at the centre of the series of 23 staged photographs Her research brought her to slavery, the “cruellest period in human history”, which is often just associated with the men who were forced across oceans to form workforces abroad. Women, she noticed, were largely invisible, their stories untold. With that in mind, Tulizo placed women at the centre of her series of 23 staged photographs called Mababu (“ancestors” in Swahili).

Rolling power outages left hospitals and water pumping stations without electricity and households without running water, interrupted critical medical procedures, and contributed to a nationwide shortage of drinking water. "Instead of blaming sabotage, the authorities should address the root causes of the failure and ensure that everyone, including detainees, has access to water, electricity, and methods for cooling." stories.title: Algérie: le président Tebboune fustige la flambée des prix alimentée qu'il impute aux «intermédiaires»

stories.title: À la Une: le bilan de la visite de Romuald Wadagni en France
stories.summary: Revue de presse Afrique À la Une: le bilan de la visite de Romuald Wadagni en France Publié le : 06/10/2026 - 10:44 Le président français Emmanuel Macron avec le président béninois Romuald Wadagni, avant une cérémonie de signature à l'Élysée, à Paris, le 5 octobre 2026. © AFP - AURELIEN MORISSARD Publicité La première visite de Romuald Wadagni en France depuis son investiture. Pour La Nation, journal béninois, « cette audience reste un temps fort de la première visite officielle qu’effectue le chef de l’État » à Paris, elle entre « dans une dynamique de dialogue et de concertation entre les deux pays. » « Pour Cotonou comme pour Paris, cette visite revêt une importance particulière , analyse ensuite La Nation , elle offre l’occasion de consolider des liens historiques tout en explorant de nouvelles pistes de collaboration adaptées aux défis actuels. À travers cette séquence diplomatique de haut niveau, Romuald Wadagni entend donc poursuivre sa stratégie d’ouverture et de diversification des partenariats, dans un contexte marqué par une volonté commune de renforcer les relations entre les deux pays. » La signature de plusieurs accords financiers entre Cotonou et Paris La Nouvelle Tribune , autre titre béninois, en compte trois, dans les domaines de l'électricité, de l'agriculture et de la santé. « Celui qui retient l’attention est le programme consacré à l’extension et au développement des réseaux électriques. Abiy Ahmed rempile pour un nouveau mandat de Premier ministre en Éthiopie Quatre mois après les législatives, le dirigeant éthiopien a été reconduit à la tête du gouvernement fédéral, par son parti, le parti de la Prospérité, qui a obtenu 87 pour cent des sièges à la Chambre des communes , rappelle l'hebdomadaire éthiopien Addis Fortune. « Une réélection en plein regain de tensions avec le Tigré , pointe Afrik.com , alors que les combats ont repris dans le nord du pays entre les forces fédérales et le Front de libération du peuple du Tigré, le TPLF . » Cependant, « la crise ne se limite pas au face-à-face entre Addis-Abeba et le TPLF , rappelle le site internet, les relations entre l’Éthiopie et l’Érythrée se sont également fortement dégradées ces dernières semaines. (...) Addis-Abeba accuse Asmara de soutenir les forces opposées au gouvernement fédéral, ce que l’Érythrée conteste. » Ces tensions se sont fait sentir dans le communiqué signé par le ministère des Affaires étrangères éthiopien, et publié ce lundi.

Over the past two years, Africa CDC has supported Ghana with equipment, communications and data infrastructure, operational systems and workforce development for emergency preparedness and response. The latest support brought together 50 national and subnational technical experts in Accra from 21-25 September to improve PHEOC operations management, and the use of the Incident Management System (IMS), in line with the 2022 Lusaka Call to Action on strengthening PHEOCs across Africa. Participants were drawn from the Ghana Health Service, the Ministry of Health, veterinary and environmental services, immigration and port health, local government, emergency services, the military and police. stories.summary: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, A pro-government soldier standing guard on a street in Ethiopia's Tigray region on Sunday By Teklemariam Bekit ,Â editor, BBC Tigrinya, Â and Â Jack Burgess Published 4 October 2026 Updated 5 October 2026 Rebel forces in Ethiopia's northern Tigray region have said they have temporarily withdrawn from the regional capital, Mekelle, as fighting with the national army moves towards the city. The Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), which has been running the region, said it decised to leave because of concerns about risks to civilians. stories.title: Skull fractures suggest servants of Egypt’s ancient kings were sacrificed
stories.summary: A fresco depicting a funeral procession in ancient Egypt. Photograph: DEA/F Guenet/De Agostini/Getty Images View image in fullscreen A fresco depicting a funeral procession in ancient Egypt. Photograph: DEA/F Guenet/De Agostini/Getty Images Skull fractures suggest servants of Egypt’s ancient kings were sacrificed Study of remains taken from royal cemetery at Umm el-Qa’ab appears to confirm early Egyptologist’s theory Court officials and craftspeople serving early Egyptian kings may have been sacrificed when their ruler died, according to research that found fractures in several ancient skulls. The royal cemetery of Umm el-Qa’ab near Abydos features the tombs and enclosures of the First Dynasty rulers of Egypt, and dates as far back as 3,000BC. Not only royalty were buried at the site: surrounding these structures are graves thought to belong to people associated with the royal households – including ladies, seal-bearers, inspectors and artisans.

stories.title: Anthropic report: Is Russia using AI for disinformation in the Central African Republic and elsewhere across Africa?
stories.summary: https://p.dw.com/p/5NTaF The Claude app was allegedly misused by Russian agents Image: Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto/picture alliance Advertisement In Bangui, the capital of the Central African Republic , Russian agents are said to have deliberately used the AI assistant Claude to promote pro-Russian influence. A report titled " Detecting and Countering Misuse of AI ," published by US-based company Anthropic in September, detailed how opposition politicians were monitored, propaganda content was created and disinformation campaigns were supported. The report claimed that Claude was used primarily to produce content broadcast by Radio Lengo Songo, a radio station that, according to the international investigative collective All Eyes on Wagner, is funded by Russia. The collective, made up of journalists, academics and experts, investigates the activities of the Russian mercenary Wagner Group and its successor structures, such as the Africa Corps, around the world. Pro-Russian propaganda, surveillance of the opposition The Anthropic report said the content was pro-Russian and portrayed the Central African government and the Africa Corps mercenaries in a positive light, while taking a critical stance on France and the opposition.

stories.title: Knox Chitiyo obituary
stories.summary: Knox Chitiyo left Zimbabwe in 2005 to live in the UK, where he was head of the Royal United Services Institute’s Africa programme View image in fullscreen Knox Chitiyo left Zimbabwe in 2005 to live in the UK, where he was head of the Royal United Services Institute’s Africa programme Obituary Knox Chitiyo obituary My friend and former colleague Knox Chitiyo, who has died aged 65 of bowel cancer, was a Zimbabwean academic and later an important voice in Britain on his homeland and its future. He was regularly consulted by diplomats, business people, journalists, academics and activists. From 1992 to 2003 he was a senior lecturer in war studies and military history at the University of Zimbabwe, where he co-founded the Centre for Defence Studies, serving as its deputy director. He also taught on the joint command and staff course at Zimbabwe’s National Army Staff College and at the Gweru Military Academy, helping shape the strategic thinking of a generation of officers. As intellectual space in Zimbabwe tightened under Robert Mugabe , Knox moved to the UK in 2005.

stories.summary: Figure caption, Boateng Bismark James has been preaching on buses leaving Neoplan station since 2023 By Thomas Naadi BBC Africa ,Â Reporting from Accra Published 4 October 2026 Before the morning rush begins, the sound of praise and worship fills the Neoplan bus station in Ghana's capital, Accra, as a group of Christians gather to prepare to evangelise on vehicles taking travellers across the country. Amid drumming and dancing, Boateng Bismark James leads 13 worshippers, nine men and four women, in prayer for drivers and passengers travelling to destinations across Ghana. Photograph: Valentine Benjamin View image in fullscreen Martha Agbani, centre, with some of the women planters she has trained in mangrove restoration techniques in the Niger delta, an area devastated by five decades of oil pollution. Photograph: Valentine Benjamin One green shoot at a time: the women restoring mangrove forests in the oil-ravaged Niger delta In a region of Nigeria blighted by decades of pollution, Martha Agbani and her team are not just replanting trees but regaining ownership of their lost lands and livelihoods A toxic landscape was familiar to Martha Agbani when she was growing up – the smell of crude oil in the air, rivers running black and trees dying on the banks. In Ogoniland, in Nigeria’s oil-exploited Niger delta, Agbani saw the spills rot away the mangrove forests and destroy the livelihoods of communities around her. Now, she is training women to plant them back – one fragile green shoot at a time.

stories.summary: Alan Ferguson, a fluent speaker of Swahili, worked for aid agencies in Kenya on family planning and public health View image in fullscreen Alan Ferguson, a fluent speaker of Swahili, worked for aid agencies in Kenya on family planning and public health Obituary Alan Ferguson obituary My brother, Alan Ferguson, who has died aged 79, was a Scotsman who began his working life as a geography lecturer at Nairobi University in Kenya , before working with aid agencies in that country. Alan joined the university in 1972, but left after a couple of years to teach in Britain at Cambridge University, and then in the US at NorthEastern University in Chicago. However, Kenya had got a hold on him, and he returned to work there, first for Amref , a Dutch organisation, and then GTZ, a German body, mainly in family planning and public health. Eventually he went freelance, helping various aid agencies with their work in Kenya, until a serious accident incapacitated him, forcing him to retire to Scotland. Born in Glasgow , Alan was the son of Bill, an analytical chemist, and Jessie (nee Moncrieff), a shorthand typist.

Photograph: Andrew H Brown View image in fullscreen Much of the land taken during the colonial era has remained with the political elite and foreign companies occupying huge tea plantations. Photograph: Andrew H Brown ‘They raped our country’: documentary follows Kenyans’ fight for restitution over stolen land Multinational tea companies still occupy ancestral highlands of communities displaced during British colonial era F or British colonialists, the fertile and cool uplands of central Kenya were the “White Highlands”, to be reserved exclusively for European settlers. Local communities were forced from the land, which was turned into plantations for tea and other crops. In recent decades, descendants of the displaced have fought to reclaim their ancestral land, some of which is now occupied by multinational tea companies and other large corporations.

Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP Trump administration diverts human rights funds to push far-right agenda abroad Support such as for white Afrikaners and anti-communism reveals how US is redefining what qualifies as human rights With hours left before the funding expires, the Trump administration is pushing to direct more than $175m of the state department’s flagship human rights fund to a slate of awards that includes a huge $40m grant for an anti-communism fund, support for a group advancing white Afrikaner rights in South Africa, a campaign against Brazil’s supreme court and programs that would reward ideological allies in Europe who protect “western civilizational norms”. stories.title: Five EU states plan first deportation center in Africa for 2027
stories.summary: https://p.dw.com/p/5NX1O Prospective migrants who arrived in Greece are taken into a migration hub Image: Sofia Kleftaki/DW Advertisement Deportation centers are legally contentious, expensive and the subject of political controversy: For years, Brussels has been grappling with the issue of establishing such centers outside the EU for rejected asylum seekers. Previous attempts have failed due to legal objections, but now, a "group of five" consisting of Greece , Germany , Austria , Denmark and the Netherlands believes it has overcome these hurdles . During an interview with the Greek television channel ANT1, Greece's Minister of Migration, Thanos Plevris, stated that the first of these so-called " return hubs " is scheduled to begin operations as early as the second half of 2027 — just in time for Greece to assume the EU Council Presidency. Plevris said Greece had chosen an African country but could not reveal its name yet. Diplomatic circles and media outlets close to the EU have repeatedly cited Rwanda or Uganda , but neither country has been confirmed as the location.

stories.title: Cotton Queen review – mystery, matriarchs and magic in pioneering Sudanese debut
stories.summary: Can she shape her own future? … Rabha Mohamed Mahmoud as Al-Sit and Mihad Murtada as Nafisa in Cotton Queen. Photograph: Frida Marzouk View image in fullscreen Can she shape her own future? … Rabha Mohamed Mahmoud as Al-Sit and Mihad Murtada as Nafisa in Cotton Queen. Photograph: Frida Marzouk Review Cotton Queen review – mystery, matriarchs and magic in pioneering Sudanese debut Suzannah Mirghani’s first feature contains a powerful performance by Rabha Mohamed Mahmoud as a village’s elder woman and tackles the long shadow of British imperialism and women’s rights ‘I decide my past,” says a village matriarch in this intriguingly political and poetic drama from Suzannah Mirghani, making her feature debut – and with it becoming the first Sudanese woman to direct a feature. (She was forced to cancel the original shoot in Sudan when war broke out in 2023 , moving production to Egypt.) It’s a film with things to say about the long shadow of the British empire, neocolonialism, women’s rights and female genital mutilation. But it mostly says it all without undermining its sense of mystery and shivers of magic realism. We’re in present day Sudan , where village elder Al-Sit (Rabha Mohamed Mahmoud) is an iron-willed woman not to be messed with.

stories.title: The journalist crowned king in Uganda after bitter succession dispute
stories.summary: Image source, Ngabo Amon/BBC By Basillioh Rukanga Â and Â Bella Twine ,Â BBC Focus on Africa Published 29 September 2026 Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma has been crowned king of Uganda's Tooro kingdom. The new monarch has long been a familiar face in the East African nation, where for many he was known not as the heir to the throne, but as a storyteller: a long-serving anchor and editor at the state broadcaster. But the 56-year-old - now King Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma Nyabongo I - has become the subject of media attention himself as his rise to the Tooro throne sparked controversy and widespread reactions beyond the country. Tooro is one of Uganda's four main officially recognised historical kingdoms. For the last 31 years, it had been headed by King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, who was once known as a "boy king", after ascending to the throne as an infant.

Eno Mwamba said his father, who is leader of the United National Independence Party, has been charged with treason following President Hakainde Hichilema's disputed election victory.
